218	\paragraph{Results.}
219	The detector identifies all three CIVO-positive runs (TPR = 3/3). Two of three are detected \emph{predictively}: 008d seed~0 triggers at 45K, one checkpoint before evaluation crosses the 20\% decline threshold; seed~3 triggers at 45K, a full 50K steps before decline begins. The third case (010b, Cheetah Run) involves single-step collapse (evaluation drops 80\% in one interval), and the detector fires reactively at the next available checkpoint. No checkpoint-based monitor can provide advance warning for instantaneous collapse.
220	
221	Two false positives occur among eight negative cases (FPR = 2/8, precision = 3/5 = 0.60, F$_1$ = 0.75). Run 009c (no duration embedding) develops genuine late-stage value overestimation unrelated to CIVO; the detector correctly identifies value-performance dissociation, and the alert is arguably useful despite the label mismatch. Run 009a (vanilla baseline) triggers during a transient three-checkpoint eval dip at 85K; the model subsequently recovers to 966, constituting a pure false alarm. In practice, the cost of a false alert (manual checkpoint inspection, minutes) is orders of magnitude lower than the cost of undetected collapse (wasted GPU-hours, corrupted model); moderate FPR is therefore acceptable in this application.
222	
223	All three true positives triggered before 65K steps (range 45--65K) while both false positives occurred after 85K (range 85--105K), suggesting that early-training alerts carry higher diagnostic confidence. In practice, alerts before 70K steps can be treated as high-confidence CIVO indicators; later alerts warrant manual inspection.
224	
225	\paragraph{Cross-simulator specificity (PickCube).}
226	Exp\_019b applies the CIVO-trigger configuration (trained $\dt$-embedding, subsample ON, $H{=}8$) to PickCube-v1 in ManiSkill3, a manipulation task with sparse rewards and qualitatively different dynamics from DMC locomotion. The V/E ratio exhibits an oscillatory pattern rather than monotonic divergence: it spikes to $r_t = 5.66$ at 52.5K (eval crashes from 24.9 to 3.7), then deflates to 1.38 by 72.5K as value estimates self-correct, eventually reaching 0.065$\times$ NVE at 202.5K. This spike-then-deflation trajectory prevents the acceleration condition from co-occurring with evaluation decline at any single checkpoint. When V/E accelerates during early training (22.5--32.5K, consecutive velocities $+0.50$, $+1.85$), evaluation has not yet declined (C4 fails). When evaluation does decline (42.5--52.5K), the preceding V/E velocity is negative ($-0.81$), so the acceleration condition (C3) fails. Across all 14 checkpoints evaluated through 132.5K, no checkpoint satisfies all four conditions simultaneously, and the detector correctly remains silent (TN). This confirms that the acceleration filter distinguishes transient overestimation spikes from the sustained monotonic divergence characteristic of CIVO. The result extends the detector's specificity validation to a second simulator and a sparse-reward manipulation domain.

\paragraph{Limitations.}
Four constraints bound the current detector. First, the three-checkpoint window cannot distinguish transient dips from sustained collapse (the source of the 009a false alarm). Second, the acceleration condition assumes monotonically increasing overestimation during onset; oscillatory trajectories that eventually collapse could evade detection until acceleration stabilizes. Third, the detector identifies a \emph{pattern} (rising value-evaluation ratio with declining performance) rather than a \emph{mechanism}: run 009c shows that non-CIVO pathologies produce the same signature. Fourth, threshold values ($\tau_\text{mag} = 0.49$, $\tau_\text{vel} = 0.1$) were calibrated on eleven runs across three environments; generalization to different reward scales requires further validation. The detector targets sustained CIVO patterns; transient single-checkpoint spikes (as observed in SGS-protected runs) are by design not flagged, as they do not indicate impending permanent collapse.

content.content:
1	Temporal abstraction via variable-rate imagination is a natural extension of world-model reinforcement learning, yet we find that every variable-rate configuration of DreamerV3 degrades performance, despite the success of identical $\Delta t$-conditioning in MPC-based methods. Through factorial diagnostics on two continuous-control tasks (Walker Walk, Cheetah Run), we identify the combination of trained temporal embedding and multi-rate data exposure as the causal factor and characterize the resulting failure mode: \emph{conditioning-induced value overestimation} (CIVO). The trained embedding enables the RSSM reward head to develop a $2.78\times$ prediction gap between $\Delta t{=}1$ and $\Delta t{=}2$, which the critic internalizes as optimistic values. This mechanism universally degrades performance to below 30\% of baseline across all four tested seeds ($n{=}4$), with three progressing toward full collapse and one self-correcting to a stable but degraded state. Gradient decomposition reveals that despite the reward head providing the largest gradient contribution (38--49\%), the observation decoder channel (16--22\%) carries the critical $\Delta t$-specific spatial information that drives the fidelity gap. Full-pathway gradient stopping partially prevents CIVO but succeeds in only 50\% of cases; this exposes additional mechanisms beyond gradient-mediated co-adaptation. A lightweight online detector that monitors value-to-evaluation ratio dynamics identifies CIVO onset with 100\% sensitivity (3/3 cases) and provides predictive warning before performance degradation in 2/3 cases, which supports early intervention without a reference baseline. The contrast with MPC-based methods identifies the feedback architecture (imagination-based bootstrapping versus re-planning) as the structural factor that transforms manageable model imprecision into pathological value dynamics.

8	Four further findings complicate the picture: (1)~expanded seed analysis ($n{=}4$) confirms that the same CIVO trigger universally degrades performance to below 30\% of baseline, with 3/4 of seeds progressing toward full collapse at variable onset timing and 1/4 self-correcting to a stable but degraded state; (2)~restricting imagination to $\dt{=}1$ while retaining the trained embedding does not prevent collapse, with one of two seeds failing via a qualitatively distinct non-CIVO pathway (evaluation-driven, increasing entropy); (3)~the contrast with TAWM identifies the feedback architecture (imagination-based bootstrapping versus MPC re-planning) as the structural factor that transforms manageable model imprecision into pathological value dynamics; and (4)~a lightweight four-condition rule-based monitor that tracks value-to-evaluation ratio dynamics achieves 100\% sensitivity for CIVO detection (3/3 cases) with predictive warning before performance degradation in 2/3 cases, which supports early intervention without a reference baseline run.

Every variable-rate configuration we test degrades performance catastrophically: fixed $\dt{=}2$ collapses to $14\%$ of baseline, fixed $\dt{=}4$ never exceeds $19\%$ of baseline, and a learned Gumbel-Softmax gate collapses to $11\%$. Through a factorial analysis on Walker Walk \citep{tassa2018dmcontrol}, we isolate the combination of a \emph{trained} $\dt$-embedding and multi-rate data exposure as the causal factor within the factorial design tested. This trained-and-exposed embedding enables the RSSM reward head to develop a $2.78\times$ prediction gap between $\dt{=}1$ and $\dt{=}2$, which the critic internalizes as optimistic value estimates, a failure mode we term \emph{conditioning-induced value overestimation} (CIVO). A $\nve \geq 1.5\times$ threshold (35K+ window) achieves 11/12 CIVO classification ($n{=}12$, single environment), with one non-CIVO false positive, a failure mode analogous to delusional bias \citep{lu2018nondelusional} that arises from model imprecision amplified by learned temporal conditioning. Gradient decomposition reveals a non-obvious mechanism: the reward head contributes the largest gradient share (38--49\%) but does not encode $\dt$-specific structural information, while the observation decoder channel (16--22\%) carries the critical spatial predictions that drive the RSSM fidelity gap. Reward-only gradient stopping fails (NVE $10.42\times$) despite targeting the largest pathway; full-pathway SGS that removes observation decoder gradients from the temporal embedding \sgsclaim{} (eval \sgseval{} vs.\ collapse at 40.8). \paragraph{F7: Full-pathway gradient stopping shows mixed results.}
Exp\_018 applies Selective Gradient Stopping (SGS) by detaching all non-KL gradients from $e_{\dt}$; this blocks the observation decoder pathway identified in F2 as the primary CIVO conduit. Figure~\ref{fig:civo_decomposition} decomposes evaluation returns across conditions. Trained $\dt$-embedding alone produces $-73\%$ peak and $-86\%$ final eval degradation relative to the baseline. Full-SGS seed~1 avoids collapse (eval \sgseval{}, $-51\%$ final relative to baseline) while seed~2 collapses (eval 40.8, $-96\%$); the overall recovery rate is 50\%. SGS reduces but does not eliminate CIVO risk: the gradient pathway it blocks is necessary but not sufficient for reliable elimination. Reward-only SGS (016e) fails entirely (NVE $10.42\times$). Cross-environment validation on Cheetah Run (010b, 2 seeds) confirms CIVO generalization: both seeds collapse (peak NVE $8.27\times$ and $70.64\times$, final eval 51.7 and 0.83 at 105K). Full-SGS on Cheetah Run enables recovery from transient CIVO onset (NVE $9.94\times$ at 45K, eval 4.6) to functional performance (eval 221.5 at 105K), in contrast to permanent collapse without SGS (010b: eval 51.7, 0.83 across 2 seeds). Combined with Walker results (50\% recovery rate), SGS is necessary but not sufficient for CIVO elimination. Removing the embedding on Cheetah eliminates CIVO entirely (024b, 2 seeds, NVE $< 0.2\times$, eval 96.5/77.3), replicating the Walker causal control (008f) in a second environment.
